stories.topic: Nadan Balak in the Ministry of Finance Export-Targets Meeting
stories.summary: Early in his career at the Ministry of Finance, Ajay sat in an annual meeting whose purpose was to set an export target for India. He raised his hand to say no one in the room actually does any exporting — exporting is done by private people. The target should be: what rules did we get out of the way so that private actors could export? The room treated him like a 'nadan balak' and told him he'd understand the importance of targets when he became a real policymaker.
stories.insight: A small parable of how deep the central-planner mindset runs in Indian economic policy. The state habitually claims credit for outcomes it does not produce and sets targets for activity it does not perform — and dismisses the obvious objection as naivete.

stories.topic: Jaswant Singh, Percy Mistry, and the Bombay International Financial Centre Vision
stories.summary: When Jaswant Singh was Finance Minister, he sat with Rakesh Mohan and Ajay and asked: have you thought about Bombay as a global producer of financial services? He said it would take 25 years, but Bombay had to challenge London. That conversation seeded the Percy Mistry committee, whose 2007 report 'Bombay as an International Financial Centre' worked the idea out in detail and ultimately led to FSLRC. Then everything got derailed.
stories.insight: A long-arc story of how a single political question, asked at the right time, can spawn a multi-decade policy programme — and how easily that programme can be lost. Twenty-five-year plays demand institutional persistence India has not yet built.

stories.topic: The 2019 NSE Payment Delay to Foreign Participants
stories.summary: In 2019, a stupid dispute between NSE and SEBI led to a payment delay to foreign participants on the exchange. Jayanth Varma wrote a blog post on it. For Ajay it crystallised what Percy Mistry had told him years earlier — that a financial centre can never have a payment failure, regardless of why. On that day, every foreigner thinks: 'You're a third-world country, I can't trust payments out of an Indian exchange.' And then it takes 25 years to rebuild that confidence.
stories.insight: Trust in financial infrastructure is asymmetric — built slowly, broken instantly. A single technical failure leaks the message that the institutional environment is unsound, undoing decades of work. The product a financial centre sells is not technology but credibility.

stories.topic: Percy Mistry's Lesson on Mics vs. Dollar-Yen Futures
stories.summary: A microphone, once made, has objective testable characteristics — its history of production no longer matters. But a dollar-yen futures contract held for two months is a continuous promise: the buyer in Chicago is vulnerable for those two months to the entire institutional apparatus that backs the trade — checks and balances, dispute resolution, regulators, law. Percy taught Ajay that the quality of a financial product is the quality of its institutional environment.
stories.insight: Goods are objects; financial services are ongoing institutional performances. To export financial services is to export a country's rule of law — you cannot fake it with technology, only by building durable institutions that strangers in Chicago can sleep on for two months.

stories.topic: Iceland Holding Argentina to a Draw
stories.summary: Amit recalled the 2018 World Cup, when Iceland drew 1-1 with Argentina. Iceland's population, he calculated, is about the size of Versova — not Bombay, not Andheri, not even Andheri West (which is vast and contains multitudes), just Versova. Ajay added: Iceland is 300,000 fishermen, and they stand up to mighty Argentina.
stories.insight: Country size does not bound performance. The Netherlands is the size of Haryana and is the world's third-largest food exporter; Iceland is the size of Versova and competes at the football World Cup. Outcomes are produced by institutions and skill, not by area or headcount.

stories.topic: Sharad Joshi and the APMC Lament
stories.summary: Amit invoked Sharad Joshi, the post-independence politician who fought for farmer freedom. Joshi protested the APMC monopolies that bought from farmers at one rupee and sold to consumers at twenty. He had a Marathi couplet: 'Hum saste bechke marte hain, tum mehenga khareed ke marte ho' — I die selling cheap, you die buying expensive.
stories.insight: A single line of folk verse captures what reams of welfare-economics analysis prove — that intermediating monopolies hurt both ends of a transaction. The cruelty isn't in any one party's gain but in how the state's coercive grant of monopoly extracts value from both producer and consumer.

stories.topic: China is Not a Country You Want Your Kid to Migrate To
stories.summary: Confronting admiration for the East Asian miracle, Ajay offered a simple test: if China is so great, how come your kid doesn't want to migrate to China? The developmental dictatorships of East Asia did push manufacturing and did get growth — but they were and are bad countries. The growth is not separable from the misery.
stories.insight: The migration test cuts through development-economics nostalgia. Wherever growth was forced through coercion, the resulting societies are not ones their own children want to live in. That is a price the manufacturing-romantic framework refuses to put on its scales.

recommendations.item: Worldly Philosopher: The Odyssey of Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.creator: Jeremy Adelman
recommendations.context: Adelman's biography of Albert Hirschman.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's strongest recommendation of the episode. Even where Hirschman's specific 'linkages' argument was overtaken by globalisation, the man himself led 'the world's best life' — economist, political philosopher, thinker — and his biography is the kind of life one reads to learn how to live. Ajay puts him in the same category of love as James C. Scott.

recommendations.item: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
recommendations.creator: Albert O. Hirschman
recommendations.context: Hirschman's classic short book on how members respond to decline in firms, organisations, and states.
recommendations.reason: The one Hirschman book Amit has read; he holds it up as the entry point that makes you want to read everything else. Foundational for thinking about the choices people face when an institution starts to fail them.

recommendations.item: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Episode 104, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Part 1 of this two-part series on Indian manufacturing.
recommendations.reason: The diagnostic counterpart to this prescriptive episode. Part 1 lays out twelve concrete reasons Indian manufacturing is hobbled and what should be fixed; this episode argues against treating manufacturing as a planner's special case.

recommendations.item: Beware of Industrial Policy (Episode 89, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier episode on the dangers of industrial policy.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of the case against picking winners. This episode is in many ways its sequel applied to manufacturing-as-such.

recommendations.item: The Power of Moore's Laws (Episode 87, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their episode on Moore's Law and Wright's Law.
recommendations.reason: Source of the Wright's Law / experience-curve argument that Ajay uses to dismantle the claim that productivity growth happens only in manufacturing.

recommendations.item: What's Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their deep dive into Indian agriculture.
recommendations.reason: Counterpart episode to the manufacturing argument. Agriculture isn't a low-grade activity; it is held back by the same kind of central-planning instinct that this episode warns against.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Education (Episode 54, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their EIE episode on education.
recommendations.reason: Cited as a parallel example of the correlation-as-causation trap. Schooling correlates with rich-country status, but pouring schools onto a poor country does not produce wealth.

recommendations.item: Where Has All the Infrastructure Gone? (Episode 55, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their EIE episode on Indian infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: The infrastructure analogue of the same argument: more infrastructure does not automatically produce growth, and large stranded highway investments illustrate the diminishing returns once the obvious chokepoints are solved.

recommendations.item: The Problem With Digital Public Goods (Episode 56, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their episode on digital public goods.
recommendations.reason: Another instance of the same correlation-confusion: rich-country governments use computers more, so we layer computers onto Indian government and call it progress. It isn't.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their EIE episode on floating exchange rates.
recommendations.reason: Used to explain how a faked exchange rate makes the most incompetent Indian manufacturer look globally competitive — the headline is fake export growth, paid for by a transfer from poor people in the country to the exporter.

recommendations.item: The Journey of Indian Finance (Episode 71, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their EIE episode tracing the arc of Indian financial reform.
recommendations.reason: The longer story of how the Bombay-as-IFC vision got derailed after FSLRC — essential context for understanding why the Percy Mistry agenda still sits unfinished.

recommendations.item: Invisible Infrastructure (Episode 82, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their EIE episode on invisible institutional infrastructure.
recommendations.reason: Amit predicts this phrase will appear in the title of a future Ajay book. The episode anchors the argument that beyond visible roads and ports, advanced economies run on invisible infrastructure — norms, contracts, dispute resolution — that India still needs to build.

recommendations.item: A petty money dispute holds market to ransom
recommendations.creator: Jayanth R. Varma
recommendations.context: Jayanth Varma's blog post on the 2019 NSE-SEBI dispute that delayed payments to foreign participants on NSE.
recommendations.reason: The contemporaneous account of the moment that re-taught Ajay Percy Mistry's lesson — that a financial centre can never have a payment failure, regardless of who is right and who is wrong.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's foundational text on Indian economic-policy frame.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show notes; the underlying methodological frame for the entire two-part manufacturing argument — the role of the state is to do the basics and get out of the way.

recommendations.item: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on Indian agricultural policy.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show notes alongside Sharad Joshi's APMC critique — the long-form articulation of the argument that the state's coercive role in agriculture, not the farmer's lack of skill, is the source of the problem.

recommendations.item: Poker and Life (Episode 38, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their episode on poker.
recommendations.reason: Referenced when Amit insists, after Ajay's quip about hanging out with poker players, that he was in fact a serious thinker about the game — and that the EIE episode shows it. Listed in the show notes.

recommendations.item: Life Lessons
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An online course taught jointly by Amit and Ajay.
recommendations.reason: Plugged in the episode's intro and listed in the show notes as the live course where they teach the broader frames that animate EIE.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Pillars of the Old Manufacturing Dogma
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay reconstructs the 1960s-80s development-economics consensus from four pillars: (1) Nicholas Kaldor's correlation between manufacturing growth and GDP growth; (2) Wright's Law / experience curves — manufacturing is the unique site of productivity growth as you produce more units; (3) Albert Hirschman's linkages — manufacturing creates positive externalities that cascade across the economy, justifying state action to ignite a few candles of light; (4) Hollis Chenery's empirical regularity of structural transformation — every successful country passes through a manufacturing way-station of 20-50% of GDP. Together these crystallised into the dogma that manufacturing is a necessary phase, that the state should artificially induce it, and that services don't really count.
core_ideas.quote: Development success will go through this script — you will have to go through a manufacturing phase; it is seen as a necessary way station, and then you can graduate to other things.

core_ideas.concept: Hirschman Was Right About Linkages — But Linkages Went Global
core_ideas.explanation: Hirschman's intuition that manufacturing thrives on dense linkages was correct; it is the country boundary that has dissolved. A modern car has German body, Czech seats, Romanian wiring, Pune (KPIT) operating-system software. Production is now global value chains (GVCs); the linkages no longer step into the footprint of any one country's policy. So the correct prescription isn't 'state action to seed candles of light' — it is to remove every friction (passports, visas, PMLA, ED, current-account restrictions, capital-account restrictions, cross-border payments) that interferes with deep integration into the world economy.

The deepest mistake of development economics is treating crude historical correlations as causal levers. Chenery saw correlations between manufacturing share and growth; Kaldor saw correlations; the schooling crowd saw correlations between education and rich-country status; the infrastructure crowd saw the same; the digital-public-goods crowd saw the same. Each became a delusional theory of change. Rich countries have lots of schooling, good infrastructure, computer-using governments, and historical manufacturing booms — but these are downstream consequences of becoming rich, not exploitable inputs. The actual essence of growth is peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice; the rest follows over a hundred-year journey.
core_ideas.quote: Just because you see a correlation, it's not exploitable.

core_ideas.explanation: If you subsidise something, it grows — but that is not real growth. A faked exchange rate makes the most incompetent Indian manufacturer globally competitive on paper, generating headline export growth that is in fact a transfer from the country's poor to its exporters. The same logic applies to PLI-style subsidies for any sector. Real growth has to emerge organically from a self-organising system of self-interested people who are choosing manufacturing because it is optimal for them — not because the state has tipped the scales.
core_ideas.quote: If you subsidise something, it will grow. But that is not growth.

core_ideas.concept: Modern Manufacturing Is High-Skill, Not a Refuge for the Unskilled Peasant
core_ideas.explanation: The romantic vision of factories absorbing tens of millions of unskilled village workers is over. Modern manufacturing runs on computer-numerically-controlled lathes, automation, and English-language programming manuals. The minimum bar is non-trivial. Beyond skill, modern manufacturing demands a whole set of social norms — show up at 9 a.m., work for eight hours, no drunkenness or violence — that India's young men in particular often lack. We must stop hankering for a low-skill manufacturing world that no longer exists and play the high-skill game that does.
core_ideas.quote: There is only a high-skilled game that is available, and we have to play that game.

core_ideas.concept: There Is No Clear Line Between Manufacturing and Services
core_ideas.explanation: The boundary that animated old development economics has collapsed. Rolls-Royce sells engines as a service — billed by the hour, with the firm doing maintenance, telemetry, and on-site fixes. John Deere tractors are sensor platforms that probe soil, send telemetry to a Hyderabad call centre, and deliver agronomic advice. Kirit Parikh's framing: once you have enough food, you want the best chef; once you have enough clothes, you want the best designer. The output of a modern economy is fused goods-and-services, and trying to draw a manufacturing/services line for policy purposes is increasingly meaningless.
core_ideas.quote: It's not a tractor, it's not a machine, it's not a good anymore. It's a rich, complex agricultural productivity service.

core_ideas.concept: Services Are Now More Tradable Than Goods
core_ideas.explanation: The old argument for manufacturing's special place rested on tradability — a ball-bearing is dense compact value that ships easily, a haircut doesn't. Fibre optics changed everything. Today services are arguably more tradable than goods: financial trades flow instantly to Chicago, software flows instantly to anywhere. The constraints are political, not technological — visa rules, capital controls, restrictions on foreign lawyers and accountants. The Indian record proves it: over a decade, goods exports grew 38% nominal (about 0.5% real per year), services exports 126%. India is the ground zero where the old development theory is being destroyed.
core_ideas.quote: Services today are more tradable than goods.

core_ideas.concept: The Quality of a Financial Product Is the Quality of Its Institutional Environment
core_ideas.explanation: Percy Mistry's deep teaching. A microphone is an object: once made, it has objective testable characteristics and its production history is irrelevant. A two-month dollar-yen futures contract is an ongoing promise: the buyer remains vulnerable to the institutional apparatus that backs it — checks and balances, dispute resolution, regulators, written and unwritten constitutional discipline. To export financial services is therefore to export rule of law. Bombay can be a global financial centre only when a buyer in Chicago can sleep on a 1000-crore Indian-exchange position for two months without worrying.
core_ideas.quote: The quality of the financial product is the quality of its institutional environment.

core_ideas.concept: The Wankhede Stadium Analogy — Umpires, Not Facilities
core_ideas.explanation: Imagine India builds the world's best cricket stadium with the most amazing facilities — but the umpires are bent. No top team will come and play. The British exported Wimbledon; foreigners always win at Wimbledon. That is the glory of Britain — they built rule of law, the rules of the game, the trust of the world that British common law would always deliver, and that the unwritten constitution would prevent the excesses of state power. India can have best-in-class technology, the best traders, the densest concentration of derivatives talent in Bombay's coffee shops — but until the institutional umpires are correct, the world will not bring its money to play here.
core_ideas.quote: It's not the technical characteristics of the stadium. The umpires are key.

core_ideas.explanation: Even good law produces good behaviour only when norms reinforce it. An umpire should feel embarrassed when they go home and a friend says, 'What the hell were you doing?' Judges behave better when researchers blog critical analyses of their orders. Building umpires is not just a legislative act; it is a long cultural project of respect, criticism, and an endless striving to do better. India's invisible-infrastructure deficit is not solved by passing laws — it is solved by building the norm-bearing communities that hold law-bearers to account.
core_ideas.quote: Umpires are not made just by law, they are made by people, they're made by respect.

core_ideas.concept: Agriculture Is Not Dull — It Is a Site of Productivity Growth
core_ideas.explanation: The romantic-peasant view of agriculture is as outdated as the romantic-peasant view of manufacturing. The Netherlands has the area of Haryana (or Kerala) and is the world's third-largest food exporter at 140 billion USD a year. Modern agriculture is indoor farming, agricultural robots, genetic engineering, complex post-harvest logistics — moving lychees from Bihar to Tokyo. India already has 43 billion USD of food exports vs 34 billion USD of textile and apparel exports — even on the labour-intensive cliché, food is bigger. There is nothing inferior about agriculture; the right state job is to do the basics and get out of the way.
core_ideas.quote: Don't ever tell me that agriculture is a dull, ditchwater subject.

core_ideas.concept: Peace, Easy Taxes, and a Tolerable Administration of Justice
core_ideas.explanation: Adam Smith's old line, repeatedly invoked by Ajay as the irreducible job description of the state. Don't pick winners. Don't favour manufacturing over services or services over agriculture. Don't run an industrial policy. Do the basics: physical safety, sound money, predictable taxation, working courts. Everything else — what people produce, what trades, what gets exported — emerges organically from self-interested individuals who are far better placed than any planner to know what to do. The state's role is to lay foundations and then be neutral.
core_ideas.quote: Peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice.

core_ideas.concept: The East Asian Miracle Was Not Worth the Cost
core_ideas.explanation: When admirers of the East Asian miracle invoke developmental dictatorship as a model, Ajay applies a simple test: if China is so great, how come your kid doesn't want to migrate to China? Yes, those countries did push manufacturing and did get growth — but the growth was inseparable from a way of life Indians do not want. It is not a model to emulate; it is not even a country whose citizens (or yours) want to live in it. The romance of the miracle filters out the misery that produced it.
core_ideas.quote: If China is so great, how come your kid doesn't want to migrate to China?

core_ideas.concept: The Map Is Always Out of Date
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's framing of why old development orthodoxy persists. The world changes faster than the people who think about it. Intellectual maps lag the territory by decades — and the older the map, the more confidently it is taught. The lesson for young economists: be cautious about correlations and causality, watch for the historical conditions that produced your priors, and update your map even when the established cartographers refuse to.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on renaming the show given Ajay's mood swings: 'We are going to rename the show — Everything is a Roller Coaster Ride.'

Amit on Ajay's de-escalating rage between off-camera and on-camera: 'Ten minutes ago, before we started the shoot, he was using words like rage and fury. He was then a volcano. He is now a flickering candle.'
Ajay on development economists: 'Development economists are a bit of a creepy bunch.'
Amit's mock-tractor pickup line: 'If you are a man who gets turned on by farm vehicles — what would those vehicles be called?' (set up to riff on John Deere as 'Tractor Dear').

Amit on his own dazzling inadequacy as a derivatives trader: 'You said I hang around with derivatives traders, and you, Amit Varma, hang out with people who talk about poker, thus making me sound so degenerate. I retired from poker in 2015.'

Amit on the trade-size shift in his own life: 'I was on this roller coaster high feeling really good, but you brought me crashing down — I have never traded in futures or options, and I have much closer to a thousand rupees than two thousand crores. But much, much closer.'

Amit's protective aside about umpires: 'I want to tell gentle readers that when he talks about umpires, he is not implying that Indian umpires are bad. Indian umpires are the best umpires. Great umpires.'

Amit's Versova bit on Iceland: 'Iceland was the size of Versova. Not Bombay, not Andheri, not even Andheri West, because Andheri is vast and contains multitudes, but freaking Versova. So from this we can come to the conclusion that football and food have more in common than you think.'

Amit's pomp-of-virtue moment, on Ajay's metric for goodness: 'Ajay's metric for goodness was — how many episodes of Everything is Everything have you seen? At noon every Friday, even if you were 100% good at 11:59, you get a little less good because a new episode is out. But at double speed or triple speed — now the YouTube app on the phone and the iPad allows you to watch at 3x — you can actually cover that gap very fast.'
Nicholas Kaldor's laws of growth — the 1950s-60s observation that manufacturing growth correlates with GDP growth, used here as the founding myth of the manufacturing-first dogma.
Wright's Law / experience curves — invoked as the basis of the (false) claim that productivity growth happens uniquely in manufacturing.

Albert O. Hirschman's 'linkages' and 'unbalanced growth' — the seminal idea that manufacturing's positive externalities justify state action; updated here as still right but globalised beyond country borders.

Hollis Chenery's empirical regularity of 'structural transformation' — the cross-country claim that every successful country goes through a manufacturing way-station, central to old development orthodoxy.
James C. Scott — invoked alongside Hirschman as one of the great thinkers Ajay loves, in a parenthetical declaration of intellectual loyalties.

Sharad Joshi's Marathi farmer-couplet — 'Hum saste bechke marte hain, tum mehenga khareed ke marte ho' (I die selling cheap, you die buying expensive) — used to capture the double-loss imposed on farmers and consumers by APMC monopolies.
Adam Smith's 'peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice' — the irreducible job description of the state, repeated as the right alternative to industrial policy.
Wimbledon and British common law — the example of how Britain's institutional excellence (rather than home-team protection) made it the world's tennis capital.
Kirit Parikh's framing of services rising in GDP — 'once you have enough food to eat, you want the best chef; once you have enough clothes to wear, you want the best designer.'
Rolls-Royce 'engine-as-a-service' — the firm that bills you for the engine for one hour, used here as the canonical proof that the manufacturing/services boundary has collapsed.
John Deere as a sensor platform — the agricultural-equipment maker whose tractors download firmware over the internet, sample soil, send telemetry to call centres, and deliver agronomic advice.
